title: Observe and Report
full_review:
Shopping center security, which provided the premise for the good-natured spoof "Paul Blart: Mall Cop," gets far darker treatment in "Observe and Report" (Warner Bros.), a brooding comedy.

While writer-director Jody Hill's intense satire of self-delusion scores a few oddly poignant moments, these are overwhelmed by nonstop vulgarity, sadistic violence and wayward sexual humor.

Seth Rogen plays frustrated security officer and would-be policeman Ronnie Barnhardt, whose ambition to join the force has as much to do with his desire to tote a gun as to protect the public.

As a disastrous screening interview with a police department psychologist eventually reveals, Ronnie is an unsettling combination of Travis Bickle from "Taxi Driver" and J.D. Salinger's Holden Caufield. His daily routine includes looking after his alcoholic mother (Celia Weston), with whom he still lives, and pining for cosmetics shop girl Brandi (Anna Faris), an airhead.

When his domain is threatened, in quick succession, by an exhibitionist and a thief, Ronnie's blundering investigation brings him into conflict with no-nonsense Detective Harrison (Ray Liotta). In keeping with the overall mood, Harrison's frustration with Ronnie's inept methods degenerates into mean-spirited persecution, as he plays on Ronnie's sadly inflated aspirations.

Along with a few scenes of surprisingly bloody mayhem -- Ronnie confronts, by turns, a gang of drug dealers and a posse of Harrison's officers -- there's also a good deal of tasteless humor involving Brandi's uninhibited lifestyle. And the flasher character is, shall we say, overexposed.

Largely lost in the scramble to be outrageous is a promising story line about gentle mall barista Nell (Collette Wolfe), whose kindly attentions Ronnie ignores in his single-minded pursuit of Brandi. Even this subplot is marred, however, by the script's ambivalent treatment of Nell's religiously motivated commitment to premarital chastity.

The film contains graphic nonmarital sexual activity, full nudity, drug and alcohol use, pervasive rough and crude language, and a few profanities. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.
